topic.subject: science
topic.title: Metals and non-metals
topic.scope: physical properties, reactions with oxygen, water, acids, displacement, reactivity, uses, corrosion

nodes.name: Metals are generally hard and solid
Prevention via Barrier and Sacrificial Protection

misconceptions.statement: All metals are hard solids that cannot be cut with a knife.
misconceptions.why: Students generalize from common metals like iron and copper used in construction.
misconceptions.fix: While most metals are hard, sodium and potassium are soft enough to be cut with a knife.

probe.question: Can any metal be cut easily with a kitchen knife?
probe.wrong_answer: No, all metals are too hard to be cut by a knife.

misconceptions.root_belief: all members of a category share all properties

misconceptions.why: Students learn the general rule and ignore allotropes like graphite.
misconceptions.fix: Most non-metals are insulators, but graphite (a form of carbon) is a good conductor of electricity.

probe.question: Which non-metal is used in making electrodes because it conducts electricity?
probe.wrong_answer: None, because non-metals do not conduct electricity.

misconceptions.root_belief: categories are mutually exclusive and absolute

misconceptions.statement: When a metal reacts with acid and disappears, it has been destroyed or turned into liquid.
misconceptions.why: Students equate 'dissolving' or 'disappearing' with the destruction of matter.
misconceptions.fix: The metal reacts to form a salt and hydrogen gas; the metal atoms are now present as ions in the solution.

probe.question: What happens to the magnesium ribbon after it reacts completely with HCl?
probe.wrong_answer: The magnesium is destroyed and no longer exists in any form.

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist
misconceptions.source_hint: Rosalind Driver's children's ideas in science

misconceptions.statement: All metal oxides are basic in nature.
misconceptions.why: NCERT introductory chapters often simplify the rule before introducing exceptions.
misconceptions.fix: Most metal oxides are basic, but some like aluminium oxide and zinc oxide show both acidic and basic behavior (amphoteric).

probe.question: How would aluminium oxide react with a strong base like Sodium Hydroxide?
probe.wrong_answer: It won't react because both are basic.

misconceptions.root_belief: one category has only one chemical nature

misconceptions.statement: Rusting is just a layer of dirt or mud that sticks to the iron.
misconceptions.why: The color and texture of rust resemble dried mud or soil.
misconceptions.fix: Rust is a new chemical substance (hydrated iron oxide) formed by the reaction of iron with oxygen and water.

probe.question: Can you turn rust back into iron by simply washing it with water?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it is just dirt on the surface.

misconceptions.root_belief: appearance defines the identity of a substance

misconceptions.statement: In a displacement reaction, the 'stronger' or 'heavier' metal wins.
misconceptions.why: Students use anthropomorphic language or confuse density/mass with chemical reactivity.
misconceptions.fix: Displacement depends on chemical reactivity (ease of losing electrons), not the physical weight or strength of the metal.

probe.question: Why does Zinc displace Copper from Copper Sulphate?
probe.wrong_answer: Because Zinc is a stronger and heavier metal than Copper.

misconceptions.root_belief: physical strength determines the outcome of interactions

misconceptions.why: Rusting of iron is the most visible and commonly discussed form of corrosion in daily life.
misconceptions.fix: Many metals corrode; for example, copper develops a green coating and silver turns black when exposed to air.

probe.question: Does a copper vessel change color over time when kept in the kitchen?
probe.wrong_answer: No, only iron changes because only iron can corrode.

misconceptions.root_belief: a specific example represents the entire process

misconceptions.statement: Any object that makes a sound when hit is sonorous.
misconceptions.why: Students use the everyday meaning of 'making sound' instead of the specific 'ringing' property.
misconceptions.fix: Sonorous refers specifically to the property of producing a deep, ringing sound, which is characteristic of metals.

probe.question: Is a wooden block sonorous because it makes a 'thud' sound when hit?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it produces a sound.

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

misconceptions.statement: Hydrogen is a metal because it is included in the reactivity series of metals.
misconceptions.why: Its placement alongside metals in the series leads to the assumption of metallic identity.
misconceptions.fix: Hydrogen is a non-metal; it is included in the series because it also loses an electron to form a positive ion, like metals.

probe.question: Is Hydrogen a metal or a non-metal?
probe.wrong_answer: It is a metal because it is in the reactivity series.

misconceptions.root_belief: position in a list implies identical category

misconceptions.statement: All metals react with dilute acids to produce hydrogen gas.
misconceptions.why: Students overgeneralize the reaction of active metals like Zinc or Magnesium.
misconceptions.fix: Less reactive metals like Copper, Silver, and Gold do not react with dilute acids to release hydrogen.

probe.question: What happens when you put a copper wire in dilute Hydrochloric acid?
probe.wrong_answer: It will produce bubbles of hydrogen gas.

misconceptions.root_belief: all members of a group behave identically

misconceptions.statement: Rusting is a physical change because the iron just changes color.
misconceptions.why: Students focus on the visible color change and ignore the formation of a new chemical compound.
misconceptions.fix: Rusting is a chemical change because iron reacts with oxygen to form a new substance, iron oxide.

probe.question: Is the formation of rust a physical or chemical change?
probe.wrong_answer: Physical change, because the iron is still there, just a different color.

misconceptions.root_belief: changes in appearance are only physical

misconceptions.why: Students learn about Carbon dioxide and Sulphur dioxide but miss neutral oxides.
misconceptions.fix: While many non-metal oxides are acidic, some like Carbon monoxide (CO) and Water (H2O) are neutral.

probe.question: Is Carbon Monoxide an acidic oxide?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it is an oxide of a non-metal.

misconceptions.root_belief: a general rule has no exceptions
